http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/31/exclu.text: Nearly six months after military conflicts broke out involving the United States, Israel, and the Islamic Republic, a reinstated US naval blockade off Iran's southern coast has brought the nation’s primary commercial lifelines to a virtual halt.Following a brief one-month pause after the Islamabad Memorandum, maritime enforcement resumed in mid-July. Since then, the chokehold on the Persian Gulf has disrupted over 80% of Iran's heavy imports and non-oil exports.With official inflation nearing 70% — and point-to-point food inflation surging to an unprecedented 128% in recent history — alongside a nearly 40% drop in non-oil trade compared to pre-war levels, ordinary citizens are left carrying the crushing financial weight.In an exclusive series of interviews with Euronews Farsi, Iranian citizens across various sectors described how the blockade has dismantled their livelihoods, forced household austerity, and reshaped daily life.Stranded cargo and soaring freight ratesThe maritime blockade has devastated logistics networks that rely on southern ports like Bandar Abbas. Gisoo, a 45-year-old international shipping specialist based in Tehran, works directly with container movements."Since the war began, maybe one out of ten cargo ships leaving China actually reaches Iran," Gisoo told Euronews."Containers that used to take 35 days now sit stuck in Hong Kong, Karachi, or Jebel Ali for months. UAE ports are no longer allowing Iranian dhows to dock."Maritime freight rates jumped from $3,000 to nearly $10,000 per container, while overland transport from China now costs at least $16,000. Rerouting cargo via Mersin in Turkey has created massive bottlenecks, leaving shipments stranded for weeks while storage fees accumulate.Land routes also require multiple unloadings and reloadings, which frequently damage sensitive goods.Because Gisoo's income relies on commissions per completed shipment, her earnings have plummeted, she added.Regarding the political fallout, Gisoo voiced scepticism about sudden systemic change, stating that fear from previous crackdowns keeps most people from taking to the streets.Desert borders and maintenance chaosWith operations at Bandar Abbas down from thousands of daily truckloads to a mere trickle, drivers have been forced to rely on poorly equipped land crossings like Rimdan on the border with Pakistan.Aras, a 60-year-old long-haul trucker from Kermanshah, described the Rimdan border as essentially lawless."Bandar Abbas is dead. Cargo from Pakistan now enters through Rimdan, but that border lacks basic infrastructure — no facilities, no dust control, just extreme heat," Aras told Euronews Farsi."Fetching a load from Rimdan to Tehran pays around 250 million tomans (€1,086), but few drivers are willing to go."Aras further detailed how operational costs for vehicle upkeep have skyrocketed under the blockade. For instance, a pair of heavy truck tyres surged from 35 million tomans (€152) before the war to 250 million tomans (€1,086) today, he said.Routine maintenance has become similarly unmanageable, with basic oil changes rising from 6 million tomans (€26) to 21 million tomans (€91), while servicing newer truck models now costs up to 70 million tomans (€304) per session, he added.Required spare parts for modern trucks have virtually disappeared from the market, leaving broken vehicles completely out of commission, he warned.If the blockade persists for another two months, widespread domestic shortages are inevitable, he added. He believes that if economic pressure forces families to the edge of starvation, widespread public protests could ultimately break the status quo. Emptying markets and shrinking mealsThe blockade’s ripple effect has severely eroded everyday consumers' purchasing power, driving up the cost of basic food items and essential medical supplies.Mansour, a 40-year-old auto technician and father of two in Tehran, told Euronews Farsi that foot traffic in local grocery stores has visibly plummeted. People are forced to strip away every non-essential expense just to get by, he observed.His own family has stopped buying meat, chicken, and rice in meaningful quantities, relying instead on bread-based meals, he said.At his auto repair shop, the price of basic motor oil rose from 1.8 million to 2.8 million tomans (€12), leaving him with almost no customers over the past two weeks, he added.Mansour said he expected the blockade to spark renewed public protests, although he anticipated heavy security responses.Hamid, a 46-year-old footwear vendor in Tehran, said the trade shutdown showed almost immediate results."The blockade’s impact is absolute. Critical medical supplies, like haemophilia treatments, have become virtually unobtainable," Hamid told Euronews Farsi."The surge in fuel and transit costs is devastating millions who rely on ride-hailing services like Snapp to feed their families.""When working-class people can no longer afford bread for their children, the pressure becomes uncontainable.", Hamid told Euronews.The widespread poverty visible on Tehran's streets has caused Hamid profound anguish. While he dreaded the hardship of ongoing blockades, he said he viewed fundamental change as the only long-term exit from systemic stagnation.Small businesses facing bankruptcyEven domestic businesses that rely on locally produced goods are getting squeezed by indirect supply chain shocks.Mohammad, a 40-year-old restaurant owner operating outside Tehran, told Euronews Farsi that his business has lost roughly 60% of its customers since the war and blockade began.Because imported beef and rice have disappeared from the market, prices for domestically produced meat and staples have naturally surged, he explained.At the same time, rising plastic costs have driven up beverage prices, while his restaurant's monthly utility bills have jumped to 10 million tomans (€43.40).To keep his remaining customers, he sells a beef koobideh platter for 500,000 tomans (€2.17) — a price that yields virtually zero profit margin, he admitted.Several neighbouring eateries have already closed down because they could not cover rent and electricity, he added.If the blockade continues through the end of the year, independent operators will face total bankruptcy, Mohammad warned, predicting that escalating costs will likely drive renewed civil demonstrations within months.

https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: Bellway is aiming to build between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year. Photograph: Steve Parsons/PA View image in fullscreen Bellway is aiming to build between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year. Photograph: Steve Parsons/PA Construction industry Burnham’s Your First Home scheme ‘could boost Bellway’s house output by 10%’ Help-to-buy initiative for England could slow market while first-time buyers wait for launch, builder admits Business live – latest updates Julia Kollewe Tue 13 Oct 2026 07.59 EDT Last modified on Tue 13 Oct 2026 08.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The new Your First Home programme for first-time buyers could increase the number of houses British builder Bellway produces each year by 10%, its boss has said. Faced with a chronic shortage of homes, the government has made housing one of its top priorities and Andy Burnham’s surprise announcement of the YFH scheme a fortnight ago sent housebuilders’ shares soaring by more than 10%. Jason Honeyman, who has led Bellway since 2017, welcomed the new programme, which will be more targeted than previous help-to-buy initiatives. It features household income caps to exclude those with big salaries, and price caps to ensure people can only buy modest houses. How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fences Read more Full details, including the launch date, are expected be announced by John Healey in his first budget as chancellor on 28 October. YFH applies only to England and is for prospective first-time buyers hoping to buy a new-build flat or house. They will be offered a government-backed equity loan worth 20% of the purchase price and the minimum deposit the buyer will have to put down will be just 2.5%. While the scheme has the potential to “provide significant support for first-time buyers”, it could weigh on the market in the near term, Honeyman said, as some will want to wait for the initiative to be launched. However, he added that it could drive Bellway’s annual completions back to 10,000 homes, in the 12-month period from next September at the earliest. “Based upon our past experience with help to buy, the new scheme has the potential to boost volumes by around 10%, and with a market recovery, provide a path back to at least 10,000 homes a year and a return on equity of 15%,” Honeyman said. Bellway is targeting between ⁠9,000 and 9,400 homes in the current year, ​down from 9,695 ​last year, ‌given a lower order book and “ongoing pressures on customer demand” coupled with higher construction costs, running at between 3% and 4%. It has a forward order book of 4,981 homes worth £1.4bn, compared with 5,285 homes with a value of £1.5bn a year earlier. Bellway also expects the average selling price to be flat over the coming year at about £325,000. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The chief executive’s comments came after the company beat analysts’ expectations with revenue of £3.16bn for the year to 31 August, up 13% from the previous year. This lifted underlying profits before tax by 5.7% to £305.7m. Bellway shares rose 2% on Tuesday but are still down by more than a quarter so far this year. YFH is expected to give a shot in the arm to most big housebuilders, such as Persimmon, MJ Gleeson, Taylor Wimpey and Bellway. However, the upmarket builder Berkeley Group, which is focused on London, where prices are higher, and Vistry Group, which has pivoted towards building affordable and social homes, are not expected to get much help from the initiative. https://praguemonitor.com/pm/briefings/c.text: Czechia Business Prague Housing Europe & World Work & Life Briefings Key points Public health insurance runs through insurance funds (zdravotní pojišťovny), the largest being VZP; you register with a GP and a dentist. Many costs are covered in full, but some items carry a doplatek (co-payment) or a fee, and some services are paid for outright. In an emergency, 155 reaches the ambulance service and 112 the general emergency line (as of 2026; check the official source). On this page 6 sections The insurers Primary care Pharmacy and prescriptions Sickness and leave Insurance for foreigners Asking in English Most foreigners meet Czech healthcare vocabulary at a reception desk with a queue behind them. The receptionist asks for your kartu pojištěnce and whether you are registrovaný , and each answer is a small piece of paperwork you may have put off for months. The terms below follow a typical patient's path, from insurer to surgery to pharmacy. This is a language aid, not medical advice. Cover depends on the law and on your insurer. The insurers Zdravotní pojišťovna is a health insurance fund. Czechia has a handful, and VZP ( Všeobecná zdravotní pojišťovna , the General Health Insurance Fund) is the largest. The others are called zaměstnanecké pojišťovny , employee funds, though any insured person can join them. The pojištěnec is the insured person; the plátce pojistného is whoever pays the premium, whether employer, employee, self-employed person or the state. Veřejné zdravotní pojištění is the public system. A státní pojištěnec is someone for whom the state pays the premium, such as children and other groups defined by law (as of 2026; check the Ministry of Health). Komerční pojištění is private commercial insurance, which some foreign residents must hold instead of public cover, depending on their residence status. Our guide to how health insurance works for foreigners sorts out who falls where. Karta pojištěnce is the insurance card. The Evropský průkaz zdravotního pojištění (EHIC) is the European Health Insurance Card, issued by your home fund and valid for necessary care elsewhere in the EU. Číslo pojištěnce is the insurance number, which for Czech citizens is the birth number ( rodné číslo ); foreign residents may be given a different one. Primary care A praktický lékař (general practitioner) is the doctor you register with, and registrace is the registration itself. Most residents register with a GP and a dentist ( zubař ), and women with a gynaecologist ( gynekolog ). A pediatr looks after children. Ordinace is the surgery and ordinační hodiny its consulting hours, posted on the door. Objednání is an appointment. Čekárna is the waiting room, which in many surgeries is the entire queue-management system. Ambulance in a hospital means an outpatient clinic, not a vehicle. A specialista is a specialist, and a doporučení or žádanka is the GP's referral to a specialist or laboratory. Vyšetření is an examination, odběr krve a blood draw. Pohotovost is out-of-hours emergency care, and lékařská služba první pomoci the on-call service for evenings, weekends and holidays. Záchranná služba is the ambulance service, reached on 155; 112 is the general emergency number (as of 2026; check the official source). Nemocnice is a hospital and fakultní nemocnice a teaching hospital attached to a medical faculty. See also how to register with a GP and how the system is organised . Pharmacy and prescriptions Lékárna is a pharmacy. Recept is a prescription, and most are now electronic, the e-recept : the doctor gives you a code or a printout to present at the pharmacy. Léky na předpis are prescription-only medicines, volně prodejné léky over-the-counter ones. Doplatek is the co-payment, the part of a medicine's or device's price the insurer does not cover. Doctors can specify a generic substitute, and it is worth asking the pharmacist for the cheapest equivalent. Regulační poplatek is a regulatory fee. Czechia has changed the fees patients pay at surgeries and pharmacies several times; most were abolished, and the main one left is a fee for using the out-of-hours emergency service ( pohotovost ). Check the Ministry of Health or your insurer for the current position. Some care, such as cosmetic treatment or certain dental work, is not covered and is paid in full. You will hear it called nadstandard , above standard. Sickness and leave Nemocenská is sickness benefit. The neschopenka , now an electronic record, is the doctor's certificate of pracovní neschopnost , temporary incapacity for work. Ošetřovné is a benefit for someone caring for a sick child or relative; mateřská and rodičovská are maternity and parental benefits. The details are in sick pay and sick leave and maternity and parental benefits . Preventivní prohlídka is a preventive check-up, available at intervals set by law. Očkovací průkaz is the vaccination record, zdravotní dokumentace your medical record, and zpráva z vyšetření a report from an examination, which you can request in writing. Insurance for foreigners Cizinecké pojištění is insurance for foreign nationals, sold by commercial insurers to satisfy residence-permit requirements. It is not the same as public insurance, and the difference matters once you work for a Czech employer or settle longer. Pojistná smlouva is the contract and pojistná událost an insured event. Výluky are exclusions, the part of any contract worth reading before you sign, and spoluúčast is the share you bear yourself. The Ministry of the Interior sets the residence-permit requirements, including proof of health insurance, so check its English pages for your category. Asking in English Many Prague practices have English-speaking staff, and some say so. If a word in your paperwork is unfamiliar, ask reception to write it down, then look it up on the Ministry of Health site. A translation app will tell you what doplatek means. It will not tell you how much it is. https://wcti12.com/news/local/town-of-wa.text: We’re learning more about a “vote of no confidence” in Warsaw. It happened in a Board of Commissioners meeting last night. The vote was cast against the town mayor, as well as a commissioner. During Monday’s meeting, Commissioner Cheryl Smith read a statement saying Warsaw Mayor Wesley Boykin and Commissioner Ebony Wills-Wells obtained a document including personal information such as “full name, date of birth, Social Security number, etc.” for town employees. She also said the two had the document for three weeks without telling the board. The following is Commissioner Smith’s statement, said in the meeting that was live streamed last night by community member Marvin Coe. Mayor Boykin and Commissioner Wills-Wells have stated that the document was found by a town employee in the parking lot of the town hall, but refuse to share who found the document, contending that the finder is a whistleblower, and whereas the town has spent and will continue to spend considerable amounts of money providing credit monitoring services for all town employees because it is impossible to determine which town employees are affected without a copy of the document. Commissioner Smith followed the statement by saying the board no longer has confidence in the leadership of Mayor Boykin or Commissioner Wills-Wells. The resolution of no confidence passed in a 4-1 vote, with Commissioner Wills-Wells as the only vote against it. News 12 emailed all of the commissioners tonight. So far, we have not heard back. We will update this story as we receive more information.
